title: Applied Causal Analysis
text:
Overview
These notes accompany the Applied Causal Analysis course at LMU Munich (Chair of Statistics and Econometrics). They introduce permutation tests from first principles, with a focus on their role in causal inference.

title: Applied Causal Analysis
text:
0.1 Bird’s Eye View
A classical hypothesis test requires four ingredients:

A hypothesis — a population statement. For example, \[H_0 : \beta = 0 \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1 : \beta \neq 0.\]
A test statistic to evaluate \(H_0\), denoted \(T_n\).
An approximation to the sampling distribution of \(T_n\) (e.g., the standard normal distribution).
A decision rule at a significance level \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). For example, the asymptotic test rejects whenever \[\phi_n^{\text{asy}} = \mathbf{1}\{|T_n| > z_{1 - \alpha/2}\}.\]

In these notes we replace step 3 with a data-driven critical value \(\hat{c}_n(1 - \alpha/2)\), and use the decision rule \[\phi_n^{\text{perm}} = \mathbf{1}\left\{|T_n| > \hat{c}_n\!\left(1 - \tfrac{\alpha}{2}\right)\right\},\] which enjoys additional finite-sample guarantees relative to the asymptotic test under some additional assumptions.

title: Applied Causal Analysis
text:
0.2 Advantages of Permutation Tests
Permutation tests have a long history dating back to Fisher (1935). From a modern causal inference perspective they offer three key advantages:

They remain agnostic about the data-generating process (DGP).
Their construction is the same regardless of the choice of \(T_n\).
They yield exact finite-sample Type I error control under the randomization hypothesis (see Section 4.8).

title: 2  Setup and Data Generation
text:
3.1 Environment
We begin by clearing the workspace and loading the project-specific function library. The library provides, among other things, the gen_data_PO() and group.action() functions that are central to these notes.


Load libraries and function library
rm(list = ls())

# Load required packages
library(ggplot2)

# Source the function library from the programs directory
source("../../programs/ACA_Function_Library.r")

# Set seed for reproducibility (L'Ecuyer-CMRG for parallel safety)
set.seed(42, kind = "L'Ecuyer-CMRG")








Note



The seed is fixed with the L’Ecuyer-CMRG generator. This generator is safe for parallel execution (e.g., parallel::mclapply) and ensures reproducibility across sessions.

title: 2  Setup and Data Generation
text:
3.2 Potential Outcomes Framework
The data-generating process follows a location-scale model for potential outcomes:
\[Y_i(0) \sim F, \qquad Y_i(1) = Y_i(0) + \tau_i,\]
where the individual treatment effect is
\[\tau_i = \mu_\tau + \sigma_\tau \cdot Y_i(0).\]
Setting \(\mu_\tau = 0\) and \(\sigma_\tau = 0\) imposes the sharp null hypothesis of no treatment effect:
\[H_0 : Y_i(1) = Y_i(0) \quad \text{a.s.} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad Y \perp D.\]
Treatment is assigned completely at random with probability \(p = 0.5\), so \(\{(Y_i(1), Y_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n \perp \{D_i\}_{i=1}^n\).


Generate data under the sharp null
# Generate data under the sharp null (te.mean = te.sd = 0)
data <- gen_data_PO(
  n      = 100,
  te.mean = 0,
  te.sd   = 0,
  p       = 0.5,
  type    = "normal"
)

str(data)


'data.frame':   100 obs. of  2 variables:
 $ Y: num  0.53 0.979 1.415 0.78 0.843 ...
 $ D: num  0 1 1 1 1 0 1 0 0 0 ...


Generate data under the sharp null
head(data)


            Y D
1  0.53046146 0
2  0.97916029 1
3  1.41470675 1
4  0.78032090 1
5  0.84298228 1
6 -0.06451182 0


The returned object is a data.frame with two columns:

Y: observed outcome.
D: binary treatment indicator (\(D_i = 1\) for treated, \(D_i = 0\) for control).

title: 2  Setup and Data Generation
text:
3.3 Visualising the Potential Outcomes
Under the sharp null \(Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)\), the marginal distributions of the treated and control outcomes should look similar. We can verify this:


Plot density of observed outcomes by treatment arm
Y_treated <- data$Y[data$D == 1]
Y_control <- data$Y[data$D == 0]

df_plot <- data.frame(
  value = c(Y_treated, Y_control),
  group = factor(
    c(rep("Treated (D=1)", length(Y_treated)),
      rep("Control (D=0)", length(Y_control)))
  )
)

ggplot(df_plot, aes(x = value, fill = group)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "tomato")) +
  labs(
    x     = "Outcome Y",
    y     = "Density",
    fill  = NULL,
    title = "Observed Outcomes by Treatment Arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 3.1: Kernel density estimates of the observed outcomes by treatment arm under the sharp null.





As expected, the two distributions are nearly indistinguishable when the sharp null holds.

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text: 4 The Permutation Test

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.1 The Randomization Hypothesis
Let \(W^{(n)} = (W_1, \ldots, W_n)\) denote the observed data taking values in a sample space \(\mathcal{W}\), generated by an unknown law \(P_n\). Our goal is to test
\[H_0 : P_n \in \Omega_0 \subset \Omega.\]
Let \(\mathbf{G}_n\) be a group of transformations acting on \(\mathcal{W}\), with cardinality \(M = \#\mathbf{G}_n\).






ImportantRandomization Hypothesis



The law \(P_n\) satisfies the randomization hypothesis with respect to \(\mathbf{G}_n\) if
\[W^{(n)} \stackrel{d}{=} g W^{(n)} \quad \forall\, g \in \mathbf{G}_n, \quad \text{whenever } P_n \in \Omega_0.\]
In words: under the null, permuting the data does not change its distribution.

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.2 The Test Statistic
Let \(T_n \equiv T_n(W^{(n)})\) be a real-valued test statistic chosen to detect departures from \(H_0\). In our two-sample setting we test whether the variance of the treated potential outcomes equals that of the control potential outcomes,
\[H_0 : \text{Var}[Y(1)] = \text{Var}[Y(0)].\]
The standardised variance-ratio statistic is
\[T_n = \frac{\hat{\sigma}_1^2 - \hat{\sigma}_0^2}{\sqrt{\widehat{\text{Var}}(\hat{\sigma}_1^2 - \hat{\sigma}_0^2)}},\]
where \(\hat{\sigma}_d^2\) is the sample variance in arm \(d \in \{0,1\}\) and the denominator uses the delta-method variance estimator implemented in Tn_stat_variance().


Compute the observed test statistic
Y1 <- data$Y[data$D == 1]
Y0 <- data$Y[data$D == 0]

Tn_obs <- abs(Tn_stat_variance(Y1, Y0))
cat("Observed test statistic |T_n|:", round(Tn_obs, 4), "\n")


Observed test statistic |T_n|: 0.6787

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.3 The Group Action: Permutations
Under completely randomised assignment with \(p = 0.5\), the natural group is the collection of all permutations of the treatment vector \(\mathbf{D} = (D_1, \ldots, D_n)\). Applying \(g \in \mathbf{G}_n\) to \(W^{(n)}\) reassigns treatment labels while keeping outcomes fixed:
\[(D_1, \ldots, D_n) \xrightarrow{g} (D_{\pi(1)}, \ldots, D_{\pi(n)}).\]
Since \(M = n!\) grows super-exponentially, we draw \(B\) permutations uniformly at random (Monte Carlo approximation):


Draw B random permutations via group.action()
B <- 100
perm_data <- group.action(data$D, B, type = "permutations")

# perm_data is an n x B matrix; column b contains the b-th permuted D vector
dim(perm_data)


[1] 100 100

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.4 Recomputing \(T_n\) Over Permutations
For each column \(b = 1, \ldots, B\) of perm_data we recompute the test statistic under the permuted assignment:


Recompute T_n over all B permutations
Tn_perm <- numeric(B)

for (b in seq_len(B)) {
  Y1_b <- data$Y[perm_data[, b] == 1]
  Y0_b <- data$Y[perm_data[, b] == 0]
  Tn_perm[b] <- abs(Tn_stat_variance(Y1_b, Y0_b))
}


The collection \(\{T_n(g_b W^{(n)})\}_{b=1}^{B}\) approximates the randomization distribution of \(T_n\) under \(H_0\).

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.5 The Permutation Critical Value
Fix \(\alpha \in (0,1)\). Define
\[k = M - \lfloor M\alpha \rfloor,\]
and let \(T_n^{(1)}(w) \leq T_n^{(2)}(w) \leq \cdots \leq T_n^{(M)}(w)\) be the sorted permutation statistics. The permutation critical value is
\[\hat{c}_n(1-\alpha) = T_n^{(k)}(w).\]

4.5.1 Handling Ties
Define
\[M^+(w) = \#\{j : T_n^{(j)}(w) > T_n^{(k)}(w)\}, \qquad
M^0(w) = \#\{j : T_n^{(j)}(w) = T_n^{(k)}(w)\}.\]
The exact permutation test is
\[\phi_n^{\text{perm}} = \begin{cases}
1 & \text{if } T_n > T_n^{(k)}(w), \\
a(w) & \text{if } T_n = T_n^{(k)}(w), \\
0 & \text{if } T_n < T_n^{(k)}(w),
\end{cases}
\quad \text{with } a(w) = \frac{M\alpha - M^+(w)}{M^0(w)}.\]
The function perm_test() implements this rule. It expects a vector whose last entry is the observed statistic \(T_n\):


Apply perm_test() to obtain the rejection decision
alpha <- 0.05

# Append the observed statistic as the last element
result <- perm_test(c(Tn_perm, Tn_obs), alpha)

cat("Reject H0 (1 = yes, 0 = no):", result, "\n")


Reject H0 (1 = yes, 0 = no): 0

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.6 Visualising the Randomization Distribution


Plot the randomization distribution
# Compute the critical value explicitly for annotation
all_stats  <- sort(c(Tn_perm, Tn_obs))
n_total    <- length(all_stats)
k_idx      <- n_total - floor(n_total * alpha)
cv_perm    <- all_stats[k_idx]

df_hist <- data.frame(Tn = Tn_perm)

ggplot(df_hist, aes(x = Tn)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "lightblue", colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = cv_perm,  colour = "red",      linetype = "dashed",  linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Tn_obs,   colour = "steelblue", linetype = "dotted", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = cv_perm + 0.05, y = Inf, vjust = 2,
           label = paste0("Perm. c.v. = ", round(cv_perm, 3)),
           colour = "red", size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  annotate("text", x = Tn_obs + 0.05, y = Inf, vjust = 4,
           label = paste0("|T_n| = ", round(Tn_obs, 3)),
           colour = "steelblue", size = 3.5, hjust = 0) +
  labs(
    x     = expression("|" * T[n] * "|"),
    y     = "Count",
    title = "Randomization Distribution"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)








Figure 4.1: Randomization distribution of \(|T_n|\) across \(B = 100\) permutations. The red dashed line marks the permutation critical value; the blue dotted line marks the observed statistic.

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.7 Permutation P-Value
An equivalent summary is the permutation p-value
\[\hat{p} = \frac{1}{M} \sum_{g \in \mathbf{G}_n} \mathbf{1}\{T_n(g W^{(n)}) \geq T_n(W^{(n)})\}.\]


Compute the permutation p-value
p_perm <- mean(c(Tn_perm, Tn_obs) >= Tn_obs)
cat("Permutation p-value:", round(p_perm, 4), "\n")


Permutation p-value: 0.6931

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.8 Exactness under the Randomization Hypothesis






TipTheorem (Finite-Sample Exactness)



If \(P_n \in \Omega_0\) satisfies the randomization hypothesis, then
\[\mathbb{E}\!\left[\phi_n^{\text{perm}}\!\left(W^{(n)}\right)\right] = \alpha
\quad \text{for all } P_n \in \Omega_0.\]


This result is non-asymptotic: it holds for every sample size \(n\) and does not require any distributional assumptions beyond the randomization hypothesis.

title: 3  The Permutation Test
text:
4.9 Computational Remarks
The exact construction requires evaluating \(T_n\) a total of \(M\) times. When \(\mathbf{G}_n\) is the group of all permutations of \(\{1, \ldots, N\}\), we have \(M = N!\). In base R the maximum vector length is \(2^{31} - 1 \approx 2 \times 10^9\), so exact enumeration becomes infeasible already at \(N = 13\) (since \(13! > 6 \times 10^9\)). In practice we therefore draw \(B \ll M\) permutations uniformly at random, as done above.

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text: 5 Monte Carlo Comparison
crumbs: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text:
5.1 Design
We compare the empirical rejection probabilities of two tests at significance level \(\alpha = 0.05\):



Test
Decision rule




Permutation
\(\phi_n^{\text{perm}} = 1\) if perm_test() returns 1


Asymptotic
\(\phi_n^{\text{asy}} = \mathbf{1}\{|T_n| > 1.96\}\)



Under the sharp null \(H_0 : Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)\) a.s., both tests should reject approximately \(100\alpha\%\) of the time. A rejection frequency below \(\alpha\) indicates a conservative test; a rejection frequency above \(\alpha\) indicates an anti-conservative (size-distorted) test. Anti-conservatism is particularly problematic because it means the nominal level \(\alpha\) is not controlled.
crumbs: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text:
5.2 Simulation Parameters


Set simulation parameters
n_sims <- 1000   # Monte Carlo replications
n      <- 100    # Sample size
B      <- 100    # Permutations per replication
alpha  <- 0.05   # Nominal level
crumbs: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text:
5.3 Main Loop


Monte Carlo loop: permutation and asymptotic test across S replications
# output[i, 1] = permutation test result
# output[i, 2] = asymptotic test result
output <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = n_sims, ncol = 2)

for (i in seq_len(n_sims)) {

  # 1. Generate data under the sharp null
  data_i <- gen_data_PO(n = n, te.mean = 0, te.sd = 0, p = 0.5, type = "normal")

  # 2. Observed test statistic
  Y1_i <- data_i$Y[data_i$D == 1]
  Y0_i <- data_i$Y[data_i$D == 0]
  Tn_i <- abs(Tn_stat_variance(Y1_i, Y0_i))

  # 3. Permutation distribution
  perm_i  <- group.action(data_i$D, B, type = "permutations")
  Tn_perm <- numeric(B)

  for (j in seq_len(B)) {
    Y1_j       <- data_i$Y[perm_i[, j] == 1]
    Y0_j       <- data_i$Y[perm_i[, j] == 0]
    Tn_perm[j] <- abs(Tn_stat_variance(Y1_j, Y0_j))
  }

  # 4. Store results
  output[i, 1] <- perm_test(c(Tn_perm, Tn_i), alpha)   # permutation
  output[i, 2] <- as.numeric(Tn_i > 1.96)               # asymptotic
}
crumbs: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text:
5.4 Results


Tabulate empirical rejection rates
rej_rates <- colMeans(output)
names(rej_rates) <- c("Permutation", "Asymptotic")

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Test                 = names(rej_rates),
    `Rejection Rate`     = round(rej_rates, 3),
    `Nominal Level`      = alpha,
    `Conservative?`      = ifelse(rej_rates < alpha, "Yes", "No"),
    check.names          = FALSE
  ),
  align = "lccc"
)

Plot empirical size of both tests

  geom_col(width = 0.5, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = alpha, linetype = "dashed", colour = "black", linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Asymptotic" = "tomato", "Permutation" = "steelblue")) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.12), labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  annotate("text", x = 2.6, y = alpha + 0.004,
           label = expression(alpha == 0.05), size = 3.5) +
  labs(
    x     = NULL,
    y     = "Empirical Rejection Rate",
    title = "Size under the Sharp Null"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text:
5.6 Interpretation
Under the sharp null, the permutation test should yield an empirical rejection frequency at or below \(\alpha = 0.05\) by the exactness theorem (Section 4.8). The asymptotic test, by contrast, relies on the normal approximation to the distribution of \(T_n\), which may not be accurate in finite samples.






Note



Increasing \(B\) (the number of Monte Carlo permutations) reduces the approximation error in \(\hat{c}_n(1-\alpha)\) and brings the empirical size of the permutation test closer to the nominal level.
crumbs: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test

title: 4  Monte Carlo: Permutation vs Asymptotic Test
text:
5.7 Summary of the Computational Procedure
The table below summarises the full permutation test algorithm as implemented above.








Step
Operation
Output




1
Observe \(W^{(n)}\); compute \(T_n(W^{(n)})\)
\(T_n\)


2
Draw \(g_1, \ldots, g_B \sim \text{Uniform}(\mathbf{G}_n)\)
\(B\) permutations


3
Recompute \(T_n(g_b W^{(n)})\) for \(b = 1, \ldots, B\)
\(\{T_n^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^B\)


4
Sort: \(T_n^{(1)} \leq \cdots \leq T_n^{(B+1)}\) (include \(T_n\) as \(g_1 = \text{id}\))
Order statistics


5
Set \(k = (B+1) - \lfloor (B+1)\alpha \rfloor\); \(\hat{c}_n = T_n^{(k)}\)
Critical value


6
Reject \(H_0\) if \(T_n > \hat{c}_n\)
\(\phi_n^{\text{perm}} \in \{0,1\}\)

title: 5  Permutation Test: A Visual Walk-Through
text:
6.1 Setup and Notation
Throughout this chapter we work with the two-sample problem introduced in Chapter 4. For clarity, we use the difference-in-means as the test statistic, not the difference-in-variance. As we argue during lecture, the construction of the permutation test does not depend on the choice of the test statistic. We only do it because it makes the visual the easiest to digest. Indeed, the same construction applies verbatim to any real-valued \(T_n\), including the variance-ratio statistic Tn_stat_variance() used in earlier chapters.
Concretely, let
\[W^{(N)} = (X_1, \ldots, X_m,\, Y_1, \ldots, Y_n)\]
be two independent samples with \(m = 10\), \(n = 12\), and \(N = m + n = 22\). Recall we seek to test
\[H_0 : P_X = P_Y \quad \text{vs} \quad H_1 : P_X \neq P_Y,\]
but this time using the test statistic
\[T_n\!\left(W^{(N)}\right) = \bar{X} - \bar{Y},
\qquad \bar{X} = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m} X_i, \quad
\bar{Y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n} Y_j.\]
Under the randomization hypothesis, if \(H_0\) holds then \(W^{(N)}\) and \(g W^{(N)}\) share the same distribution for every \(g \in \mathbf{G}_n\), where \(\mathbf{G}_n\) is the group of all permutations of \(\{1, \ldots, N\}\). This means we can generate auxiliary realizations \(T_n(g_b W^{(N)})\), \(b = 1, \ldots, B\), and use their empirical distribution as an approximation to the null distribution of \(T_n\).

title: 5  Permutation Test: A Visual Walk-Through
text:
6.3 What the Widget Illustrates
The five steps map directly onto the computational procedure summarised in Chapter 4:







Widget step
Formal object




Original samples
\(W^{(N)} = (X_1,\ldots,X_m,Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)\)


Observed \(T_n\)
\(T_n(W^{(N)}) = \bar{X} - \bar{Y}\)


Permutation \(b\)
\(g_b W^{(N)}\), new split into groups of size \(m\) and \(n\)


Permuted statistic
\(T_n(g_b W^{(N)})\)


Null distribution
\(\{T_n(g_b W^{(N)})\}_{b=1}^{B}\), with \(\hat{p}\) reported









NoteRemark on the choice of \(T_n\)



The widget uses \(T_n = \bar{X} - \bar{Y}\) for expository clarity. The permutation procedure — pool, reshuffle, recompute, repeat — is identical regardless of the test statistic. In Chapter 4 and Chapter 5 we use the studentized variance-ratio statistic Tn_stat_variance(), which is better suited to testing \(H_0 : \mathrm{Var}[Y(1)] = \mathrm{Var}[Y(0)]\).








TipKey Takeaway



Under \(H_0 : P_X = P_Y\), permuting the labels does not change the distribution of \(W^{(N)}\). Consequently, \(T_n(W^{(N)})\) and \(T_n(g_b W^{(N)})\) are identically distributed, and the empirical quantiles of \(\{T_n^{(b)}\}_{b=1}^{B}\) provide a valid (finite-sample exact) null distribution.
crumbs: 5  Permutation Test: A Visual Walk-Through
